common_name: Valerie Finnis Grape Hyacinth (Pale Ice-Blue Muscari)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Valerie Finnis is a pale, ice-blue sport of the common grape hyacinth, a softer color than the typical deep cobalt-blue species.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; grape hyacinth naturalizes readily and needs little care once established. Valerie Finnis bears dense spikes of small, tightly packed, urn-shaped florets in a soft, silvery ice-blue, a gentler and more unusual color than the deep cobalt-blue of the common species, blooming in mid-spring alongside daffodils and tulips. Its pale color makes it a versatile companion for pastel spring combinations where the standard deep-blue grape hyacinth might read as too strong. Foliage emerges in fall and persists through winter before the flower spikes appear in spring, then dies back by early summer; leave it undisturbed to die back naturally, and clumps will multiply steadily by offset bulbs to form larger drifts over the years.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Pink Giant is a pink-flowered selection of glory-of-the-snow with larger flowers than the typical blue species.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; glory-of-the-snow naturalizes readily under deciduous trees and in lawns. Pink Giant bears larger star-shaped flowers than the typical blue species, opening a soft, dusty pink with a paler center, among the earliest bulbs to bloom in very early spring, often flowering right alongside the last snow in colder climates. Its unusual color offers a departure from the blues and whites of most glory-of-the-snow plantings, working well combined with early crocus and snowdrops for a mixed drift of very early spring color. Allow the grass-like foliage to die back naturally after flowering before mowing over naturalized plantings, and it will self-seed and multiply by offset bulbs to form larger colonies over time.

common_name: Spring Beauty Siberian Squill (Large-Flowered Deep Blue Scilla)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Spring Beauty is the most widely sold Siberian squill selection, with larger flowers and a more vigorous habit than the wild species.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Siberian squill naturalizes vigorously under deciduous trees and in lawns, tolerating deep shade once trees leaf out for the summer. Spring Beauty bears larger, more richly colored, deep cobalt-blue, nodding, bell-shaped flowers than the wild species, opening in very early spring and often carpeting large areas once established, since it self-seeds and multiplies by offset bulbs readily. It is one of the most reliable and low-maintenance early spring bulbs for naturalizing, tolerating a wide range of soil and light conditions and largely ignored by deer and rodents. Allow the narrow, strappy foliage to die back naturally after flowering before mowing over naturalized lawn plantings.

common_name: Rubra Maxima Crown Imperial (Large Orange-Red Fritillaria)

planting.note: Plant large bulbs on their side 6-8 inches deep in fall in fertile, sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade; planting on the side helps prevent water from pooling in the bulb's hollow crown and causing rot.

directions: Plant large bulbs on their side 6-8 inches deep in fertile, sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade, since standing water in the hollow-crowned bulb quickly causes rot. Rubra Maxima produces a dramatic, tall flower stalk topped by a cluster of large, nodding, bell-shaped orange-red flowers beneath a tuft of leafy green bracts, one of the most striking and largest-flowered crown imperial selections, making a bold vertical accent unlike almost any other spring bulb. The entire plant, especially the bulb, carries a distinctive musky, skunk-like odor that most gardeners find unpleasant up close but that has the useful side effect of deterring deer, voles, and other bulb-eating animals from the planting. Leave the foliage to die back naturally after bloom to recharge the bulb for next year, and avoid disturbing or dividing established clumps, since crown imperial resents transplanting and may take a season or two to rebloom after being moved.

common_name: Wisley Blue Spring Starflower (Deep Blue Ipheion Selection)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Wisley Blue is a superior selection of spring starflower with larger, deeper blue flowers than the species.

directions: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; spring starflower tolerates surprisingly dry summer conditions once established and multiplies readily by offset bulbs. Wisley Blue bears larger, more richly colored, deep lavender-blue, six-petaled, star-shaped flowers than the plain species, held on slender stems above narrow, grass-like foliage that smells faintly of onion when crushed, betraying its relationship to the allium family. It blooms freely over several weeks in early to mid-spring, performing equally well in open sunny borders and in the light shade of deciduous trees. The bulbs multiply steadily, slowly forming dense clumps well suited to edging, rock gardens, or naturalizing in rough grass, and need essentially no maintenance once established beyond allowing the foliage to die back naturally after bloom.
